notes.meaning: The high priest asked Stephen if the accusations against him were true. Stephen was accused of speaking against God, Moses, the temple, and the law. Instead of giving a simple yes or no, Stephen began explaining the history of how God had always worked with their ancestors.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The charges against Stephen were twisted versions of things he had actually preached, such as Jesus predicting that the temple would be destroyed.

notes.meaning: Stephen addressed his listeners with deep respect as brothers and leaders. He explained that the glorious God appeared to Abraham far away in Mesopotamia, long before Abraham ever lived in Haran. This showed that God is not limited to one special country or building.

God told Abraham to leave his native land and his family behind to travel to an unknown place. Abraham obeyed on simple trust, stepping out in faith before he could see where he would end up. His obedience showed what it looks like to depend fully on God's word.

Abraham left his first home and stayed in Haran for a time. After his father died, God led him into Canaan, the very land where the council was now sitting. God guided Abraham one step at a time until he reached his new home.

God gave Abraham no property of his own in Canaan, not even enough ground to set his foot upon. Still, God promised that one day the whole land would belong to his descendants. Abraham trusted this promise completely, even though he and his wife did not yet have any children.

God warned Abraham that his family would live in a foreign land as mistreated slaves for four hundred years. This revealed that Israel's long suffering in Egypt was not an accident or a surprise to God. He knew their troubles beforehand and remained in complete control.

God promised to punish the kingdom that enslaved them and bring His people out to worship Him. God's judgment on their oppressors was an act of mercy designed to save His family. He rescued them so they could serve Him freely as His own people.

God made a covenant, which is a sacred agreement, and gave Abraham circumcision as an outward sign of that promise. Abraham circumcised his son Isaac, Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob fathered the twelve men who became the heads of Israel's tribes. Through this family, God kept passing down His holy promise.

Jacob's older sons grew jealous of their brother Joseph and sold him into Egypt as a slave. Even though his own brothers rejected him and threw him into exile, God was with Joseph. God's presence stayed near His servant even in a pagan land without any temple.

God rescued Joseph from all his troubles and gave him extraordinary wisdom. This wisdom pleased Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, who placed Joseph in charge of the royal palace and the whole country. Through God's power, an abandoned prisoner became a great ruler.

A severe famine swept across both Egypt and Canaan, leaving people everywhere without food. Jacob and his family suffered greatly and could find no way to feed themselves. This crisis forced them to look outside their promised land just to stay alive.

Jacob heard that grain was stored up in Egypt, so he sent ten of his sons on their first trip to buy food. The fathers of Israel had to travel as needy foreigners to survive. God was quietly preparing the way to save their lives in an unexpected place.

On their second visit, Joseph revealed his true identity to his brothers. Pharaoh also learned about Joseph's family and welcomed them into Egypt. The brother they had once hated and rejected became the very one who kept them from starving.

Joseph sent for his father Jacob and his entire family, totaling seventy-five people. Stephen used the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which counted additional descendants born in Egypt to reach that number. God preserved this small group and kept them safe under Joseph's care.

Jacob traveled down to Egypt and spent the rest of his life there, and his sons died there as well. The leaders of Israel's tribes lived and died as foreigners far from Canaan. They finished their earthly lives trusting in promises they had not yet seen fully completed.

Years later, the bones of the patriarchs were carried out of Egypt and buried in Shechem. Even in death, these leaders showed their deep faith in God's promises by returning to the land. They knew that their true hope rested in the future home God had promised them.

As the time approached for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham, the Hebrew people multiplied rapidly in Egypt. A tiny clan of seventy-five grew into a huge nation. God was faithfully preparing to deliver them just as He had sworn.

Eventually, a new king came to power in Egypt who had no regard for Joseph or his past service. This king forgot the great blessings Joseph had brought to the land. Because of this, he viewed the growing Hebrew population with suspicion and fear.

The Egyptian king acted deceitfully to crush and weaken the Israelites. He forced Hebrew parents to abandon their newborn boys outdoors so they would die. Yet even under such cruel oppression, God guarded His people from being wiped out.

Moses was born during this dark time of persecution, and he was especially lovely in the sight of God. His parents hid and cared for him in their home for three months to save his life. God was already preparing a rescuer at the very moment when hope seemed lost.

When his family could no longer hide him, Moses was placed outside by the river. Pharaoh's own daughter discovered the baby, adopted him, and raised him as her son. God used the royal family of the oppressor to shelter the future deliverer of Israel.

Moses was trained in all the high learning, science, and skills of Egypt. He grew into a capable leader, powerful in both his words and his actions. God used this royal education to equip Moses for the enormous tasks that lay ahead.

When Moses was forty years old, God put a strong desire in his heart to visit his Hebrew brothers. He chose to leave the ease of the royal court to see their hard labor for himself. His heart went out to his people in their suffering.

Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew slave and rushed to defend his fellow countryman. He struck down the Egyptian and killed him to avenge the oppressed worker. Moses acted out of compassion, showing that he stood with his own people rather than with Egypt.

Moses thought his fellow Israelites would understand that God was using him to bring them freedom, but they did not see it. Just like Joseph, Moses was ready to help his people, but they failed to recognize God's call on his life. Israel had a long history of failing to recognize their deliverers.

The next day Moses came upon two Israelites who were fighting each other and tried to bring peace between them. He reminded them that they were brothers who ought to care for one another rather than quarrel. He wanted to unite them instead of letting them tear each other down.

The man who was mistreating his neighbor shoved Moses away and asked who made him a ruler and a judge over them. The wrongdoer refused to accept correction and challenged Moses' right to speak. People doing wrong often turn against those who urge them to make peace.

The man asked Moses if he planned to kill him just as he had killed the Egyptian the day before. This revealed to Moses that his secret act was known and that his own people resented his leadership. Instead of supporting him, his fellow Israelites rejected his help.

When Moses realized he was in danger from both Pharaoh and his own people, he fled into the desert land of Midian. He lived there as a foreigner, married, and had two sons. This quiet exile became a forty-year season of waiting and humble preparation.

After forty years in the wilderness, an angel appeared to Moses in the flame of a burning bush near Mount Sinai. The bush burned brightly with fire but was not destroyed, showing God's holy presence. God revealed Himself in an ordinary desert bush, proving that He is not confined to any temple building.
